'''Benjamin S. Hsiao''' (born 12 August 1958) is a Taiwanese-American <!-- dual citizenship --> [[Materials Science|materials scientist]].  He served as the vice-president for research and chief research officer at [[Stony Brook University]] from May 2012 to December 2013.

==Early life and education==

Hsiao was born in [[Taipei]], Taiwan, and attended the all-boys [[Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School]]. He graduated from [[National Taiwan University]] with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[chemical engineering]] in 1980. He then earned his [[Ph.D.]] in [[polymer science]] from the [[University of Connecticut]] in 1987.<ref name="faculty">{{cite web |title=Faculty Page |url=http://www.chem.stonybrook.edu/faculty/hsiao.shtml |work=Stony Brook Chemistry Faculty |access-date=31 July 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120723012250/http://www.chem.stonybrook.edu/faculty/hsiao.shtml |archive-date=23 July 2012 }}</ref><ref name=page>{{cite web|title=Research Page|url=http://www.chem.stonybrook.edu:82/hsiaohome|access-date=31 July 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120903203216/http://www.chem.stonybrook.edu:82/hsiaohome|archive-date=3 September 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
He went on to work at the [[University of Massachusetts]] between 1987 and 1989 as a postdoctoral research fellow in the department of polymer science and engineering under the tutelage of Richard S. Stein and H. Henning Winter. Immediately afterwards, he was sought by the [[DuPont Company]] to work in the Pioneering Laboratory. He stayed with DuPont for 8 years in [[Wilmington, Delaware]] until 1997 as a senior staff scientist in the Central Research and Development Department, after which he embarked upon an academic career at [[Stony Brook University]].<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="news">{{cite web|title=Benjamin S. Hsiao Named Vice President for Research at Stony Brook University|url=http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/Benjamin_S_Hsiao_Named_Vice_President_for_Research_at_Stony_Brook_University.shtml|work=Stony Brook News|publisher=Stony Brook University|access-date=31 July 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120712101250/http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/Benjamin_S_Hsiao_Named_Vice_President_for_Research_at_Stony_Brook_University.shtml|archive-date=12 July 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Joining [[Stony Brook University]] as an assistant professor in 1997, Hsiao was promoted to full professor in 2002 and appointed to the chair of the chemistry department in 2007. It was under his leadership, that the chemistry department at Stony Brook was identified as one of the top departments in the nation, and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] for the invention of [[Magnetic Resonance Imaging]] (MRI) by the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name="pres">{{cite web|last=Stanley|first=Samuel|title=Benjamin S. Hsiao, PhD, Vice President for Research|url=http://www.stonybrook.edu/pres/message_040912.html|publisher=Stony Brook University|access-date=2 August 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120801124246/http://www.stonybrook.edu/pres/message_040912.html|archive-date=1 August 2012}}</ref><ref name="page" />

Hsiao was the vice president for research at Stony Brook University between 2012 and 2013 for 1.5 years. In this position, he was responsible for the campus-wide advancement of Stony Brook's research mission through strategic planning and oversaw the Research Foundation, supervised all university research administration activities and functions, and was the primary advocate for the university's research enterprise on a state, national and international level. His major contributions to the Stony Brook Research Office (SBRO) were in two areas: (1) greater efficiency and transparency of the research administration activities on campus, and (2) new research initiatives to advance Stony Brook's research mission on a state, national and international level.

Since 2008, he has also served as the Chang-Jiang Professor at [[Donghua University]] in Shanghai, and a guest professor at the [[Beijing University of Chemical Technology]], [[Tongji University]] and the  [[Changchun]] Institute of Applied Chemistry of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="sbupr">{{cite news|title=Benjamin S. Hsiao Named VP for Research|url=http://sb.cc.stonybrook.edu/happenings/facultystaff/benjamin-s-hsiao-named-vp-for-research/|access-date=2 August 2012|newspaper=Stony Brook Happenings|date=April 12, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160316235823/http://sb.cc.stonybrook.edu/happenings/facultystaff/benjamin-s-hsiao-named-vp-for-research/|archive-date=16 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Research==

Hsiao's laboratory at [[Stony Brook University]] aims to understand the structural, morphological development and manipulation of complex [[polymer]] systems during preparation and processing in real time at both [[molecular nanotechnology|molecular]] and [[nanoscopic scale]]s.<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="sbupr" /><ref name="pres" /><ref name="page" /><ref name=acs>{{cite web|title=American Chemical Society Profile|url=http://dgr.rints.com/faculty.cfm?id=S0014272|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=2 August 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150227004623/http://dgr.rints.com/faculty.cfm?id=S0014272|archive-date=27 February 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

His research in polymer science and engineering has led to novel [[water purification|water purification techniques]], Together with his colleague [[Benjamin Chu]], Hsiao has used combined [[electrospinning]] and [[nanocellulose|cellulose nanofibrous membranes technologies]] to produce an hierarchical non-woven pattern of different size fibers (from [[micrometers]] to [[nanometers]]) to [[water filter|filter]] water. Along with its mechanical integrity and its interconnected pores and thus high [[porosity|pore density]], these filters have high [[volumetric flow rate]]s without compromised resistance to [[fouling]]. Since such filters can have several times better [[Volumetric flow rate|water flux]], they are [[Efficient energy use|energy efficient]] and have a broad range of applications ranging from [[desalination]] to [[electricity generation|energy generation]].<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="sbupr" /><ref name="page" /><ref name="acs" /><ref name=um>{{cite web|title=Benjamin Hsiao, Stony Brook University|url=https://www.mse.engin.umich.edu/about/events/benjamin-hsiao-stony-brook-university/|publisher=University of Michigan: Materials Science and Engineering|access-date=2 August 2012}}</ref><ref name=aaas>{{cite news|title=Four SBU Professors Elected AAAS Fellows|url=http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/Four_SBU_Professors_Elected_AAAS_Fellows.shtml|access-date=2 August 2012|newspaper=Stony Brook News|date=Jan 23, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120126014253/http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/General_University_News_2/Four_SBU_Professors_Elected_AAAS_Fellows.shtml|archive-date=26 January 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=aaas2>{{cite news|title=Benjamin S. Hsiao Named a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science|url=http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/Faculty_Student_Awards_17/Benjamin_S_Hsiao_Named_a_Fellow_of_the_American_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Science.shtml|access-date=2 August 2012|newspaper=Stony Brook News|date=Jan 27, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120129160042/http://commcgi.cc.stonybrook.edu/am2/publish/Faculty_Student_Awards_17/Benjamin_S_Hsiao_Named_a_Fellow_of_the_American_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Science.shtml|archive-date=29 January 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Such [[nanofiber|nanofibrous]] formats are also useful for [[tissue engineering]] and [[drug delivery]]. As [[biodegradation]] rates and drug release rates in medical treatments are functions of [[fiber]], [[porosity]], [[Polymer#Morphology|morphology]] and chemical compositions, Hsiao and Chu have developed many useful new solutions for biomedical applications, such as [[Tissue engineering#Scaffolds|nanofibrous scaffolds]] for [[tissue engineering]] and [[bioartificial organ#Heart|heart tissue constructs]], and methods to prevent post-surgery induced abdominal adhesions.<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="sbupr" /><ref name="page" /><ref name="acs" /><ref name="um" />

As a [[materials science|material scientist]], Hsiao has focused on understanding the fundamental processes involved in the [[crystallization of polymers]]. In order to investigate [[Polymer#Microstructure|polymer structures]], [[Polymer#Morphology|morphology]] and [[Polymer#Phase behavior|dynamics]] from [[atomic spacing|atomic]] (1-20 Å) to [[microscopic scale]]s (20 - 1000 Å) in [[Real-time data|real time]], Hsiao's laboratory has come up with simultaneous [[Small-angle X-ray scattering|small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS)]] and [[Wide-angle X-ray scattering|wide-angle X-ray diffraction (WAXD)]] techniques. By nature, [[Small-angle X-ray scattering|SAXS]] probes relatively large-scale structures, in contrast to [[Wide-angle X-ray scattering|WAXD]] that deals mainly with the atomic structure of [[Crystallization of polymers|crystals]]. [[Small-angle X-ray scattering|SAXS]] includes not only the [[diffraction]] of large [[crystal structure|lattice spacing]], of the order of tens, hundreds or even thousands of interatomic distances, but also the scattering by perturbed or non-periodic structures of [[amorphous solid|amorphous]] and [[Crystallization of polymers#Properties of semicrystalline polymers|semi-crystalline materials]]. Dedicated to polymer research, the Advanced Polymers Participating Research Team (AP-PRT) was formed in 1997 by Hsiao and his colleague Ben Chu to develop a synchrotron X-ray scattering beamline (X27C) at the [[National Synchrotron Light Source]], [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]].<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="sbupr" /><ref name=sit>{{cite web|title=advanced Nanostructure Characterization Using Scattering/ Diffraction Techniques|url=https://docs.google.com/viewer?a=v&q=cache:qtmp5_lgQvsJ:personal.stevens.edu/~ffisher/nano/Hsiao_111208.pdf+&hl=en&gl=us&pid=bl&srcid=ADGEEShKqcASaUtiPXTGEIQ9gn7E8iDz_5s9GsOxEuU5sYaqn1C24dGgr29OKGcdHtW8y6rwrvvoZmE0TXSM3SAWpTUW1tU1Wzb9Gd3Ruald9-xdkgHg7gjzDR_RKZIYvJOiuxYLy1DG&sig=AHIEtbSy2KBZ6Pi9C-Wc6HK30Y07Mebqig|publisher=Stevens Institute of Technology|access-date=2 August 2012}}</ref><ref name="page" /><ref name="acs" /><ref name="um" /><ref name="aaas" /><ref name="aaas2" />

Having published more than 403 [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] scientific papers, 41 reviews and chapters in books and encyclopedias, 226 conference proceedings, more than 32 issued patents (including 18 US patents) and 18 pending applications, and edited two books, Hsiao holds an [[h-index]] of 74 with an [[ISI Web of Knowledge]] total citation number exceeding 17,000. He has given more than 244 invited lectures in universities, governmental and industrial research institutes and more than 474 presentations in national and international scientific meetings.<ref name="faculty" /><ref name="sbupr" /><ref name="sit" /><ref name="page" /><ref name="acs" /><ref name="um" /><ref name="aaas" /><ref name="aaas2" />
